title: Derivatives, Gradients & Chain Rule
interviewAnswer: A derivative measures local change; a gradient collects partial derivatives and points toward steepest increase. Backpropagation efficiently applies the chain rule through a computation graph.
why: Gradients connect loss functions to parameter updates. Backpropagation is just efficient chain-rule application over a computation graph.
intuition: A derivative tells how much an output changes when one input changes slightly. A gradient collects that sensitivity for every input dimension. The chain rule propagates sensitivity through composed operations.
deepDive: For a scalar loss L(θ), the gradient ∇θL points in the direction of steepest local increase. Gradient descent moves in the negative direction. The chain rule multiplies local derivatives along computational paths, and reverse-mode autodiff reuses intermediate values efficiently when a scalar loss depends on many parameters.
math:
If y=f(g(x)), dy/dx = f'(g(x)) g'(x)
Gradient: ∇f=[∂f/∂x₁,...,∂f/∂x_d]
Update: θ ← θ - η∇θL
workedExample: For L=(wx-y)², dL/dw = 2(wx-y)x. If the prediction is too high and x is positive, the gradient is positive, so gradient descent reduces w.
code:
import torch
w=torch.tensor(2.0,requires_grad=True)
x=torch.tensor(3.0); y=torch.tensor(5.0)
loss=(w*x-y)**2
loss.backward()
print(w.grad)
commonMistakes: Saying the gradient always points toward the minimum; it points toward local increase.
Confusing derivative computation with the optimizer update.
Ignoring non-differentiable points or numerical issues.
followUps: Why does backprop use reverse mode?
Why can gradient descent get stuck or oscillate?
production: Gradient health is a debugging signal. Track exploding/vanishing norms, NaNs, mixed-precision scaling and whether the intended parameters actually receive gradients.
